title: Assign indices of PIT requests in transport layer

timeline.body:
- Reject search requests that have both indices and point-in-time
- Assign the indices of PIT requests in the transport layer; otherwise, the indices of internal requests aren't assigned correctly

Closes #84187

I tried to make this an ActionFilter, but we need a hack for this. The new action filter must be executed before the security action filter, but the security action filter already has the lowest order (Integer.MIN_VALUE).

reply.body: I see the problem Nhat, thanks for raising this. Adding a new base method that runs before action filters makes me nervous. Possibly an alternative hack: would it work to make what SearchReqest#indices returns dynamic and extract the indices from pit if a pit is set? In that case the authorization filter would look at the right indices and we would not need to set the indices manually? I guess there can't be wildcards in there hence the authorization filter will not replace the indices in that scenario. there may be other side-effects though around going down this route.

If we make `SearchRequest#indices()` method dynamic, how would the corresponding setter behave? `SearchRequest` implements `IndicesRequest.Replaceable`. The contract for authorization code is that it will always call `SearchRequest#indices(String ..)` with the expanded indices regardless whether the expanded indices is identical to the original one. 

IIUC, in practice, Search with PIT always gets back to the identical list of indices from Authorization because it does not allow `ignore_unavailable=true`. So technically the setter can be a no-op, but I am not really comfortable with that because it feels PIT has to know how Authorization works. It also excludes the possibility to ever support `ignore_unavailable=true`. One option is to make the getter dynamically return the list indices from PIT if setter is never called, but otherwise return the value configured by the setter method (maybe this is already what @javanna suggests by "dynamic"?). The downside is inconsistency between the `indices()` method and the internal `indices` variable (till the setter is called).

I am ok with what @dnhatn has proposed. Though I'd rather add the new base method to `ActionRequest` instead of `TransportAction` because calling `ActionRequest#validate()` and `ActionRequest#prepare()` in sequence seems to be more fluent to me (it would be nice to make `ActionRequest#prepare` idempotent). 

Overall, I slightly prefer the `TransportAction` (or `ActionRequest`) approach which feels simpler.

If the decision is to go with the "prepare request" approach, I think "validation" should be called *after* "prepare". We need to make sure the request is still valid after some arbitrary preparation.

as far as I understand the pit indices never hold wildcards, and never will, because you need to first open a pit on a fixed set of indices. So the whole indices expansion and replacement does not really apply to this specific scenario. It would be great to have a different request for this scenario, but we don't unfortunately. The indices variable is only read by methods within SearchRequest that could call the indices() method instead for consistency? We could even say that the setter throws an exception in case a pit is set.

Indices expansion in authorization does not have knowledge about PIT. Its behaviour is largely determined by whether the incoming request is a `IndicesRequest.Replaceable`. If we could turn SearchRequest with PIT into a new class that does not implementing this interface, things should just work on the authorization side. I think this would be better than throwing exception in the setter method.

> Indices expansion in authorization does not have knowledge about PIT.

Correct. What I am saying is that because you need to explicitly open a PIT with a specific API call, the PIT id will always hold concrete indices and never wildcards when set to a search request, because you previously received it as part of the open pit response, so despite the search request implements IndicesRequest.Replaceable, there will never be anything to expand when a PIT id is set. You were reasoning about ignore_unavailable and wildcards expansion in your previous reply, but these don't apply to a search when a PIT id is set to it. I think this is important as it reduces the scope of how indices are resolved and should be authorized in this specific scenario. I believe this is key to finding a simple solution for the current problem. I do not think that introducing a new base method to TransportAction for this very specific edge-case is a good trade-off.

> If we could turn SearchRequest with PIT into a new class that does not implementing this interface, things should just work on the authorization side. I think this would be better than throwing exception in the setter method.

That would make things better, and maybe it is possible given that we have control over the REST action, though it looks to me as it has quite a cost in terms of added complexity and lines of code. We would need to try that to see it in reality.

> though it looks to me as it has quite a cost in terms of added complexity and lines of code.

Yeah Java does not make delegation easy. 

> You were reasoning about ignore_unavailable and wildcards expansion in your previous reply, but these don't apply to a search when a PIT id is set to it.

Right I understand PIT does not really need expansion. My previous reply unnecessarily blurred the focus. My point is Authorization code will call `Replaceable#indices(String...)` as long as the request is an instance of `Replaceable`. I don't particularly like having a special setter method for `SearchRequest` because it indicates SearchRequest knows about authorization. But I am ok with the opposite, i.e. Authorization knows more about SearchRequest because it already knows quite a bit about the requests. The following is where Authorization decides whether to expand wildcards (and in turn calls the setter method):

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/11599e1e5f269679f3b96da76760ebd90610ab1e/x-pack/plugin/security/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/security/authz/IndicesAndAliasesResolver.java#L131-L141

We can add an addition check for PIT before `if (indicesRequest instanceof IndicesRequest.Replaceable)` such as:
```java
if (indicesRequest instanceof final SearchRequest searchRequest && searchRequest.pointInTimeBuilder() != null) {
    return false;
}
```

The above check in conjunction with a dynamic `SearchRequest#indices()` getter method should work and the change is rather minimal. What do you think?

++ thanks @ywangd I misread the authorization code and you are right that indices are replaced anyways, even if there's no wildcards, which means that the approach I suggested alone would not work. Thanks for your patience. I do like the solution you proposed. ;)

+[[search-aggregations-random-sampler-aggregation]]
+=== Random sampler aggregation
+++++
+<titleabbrev>Random sampler</titleabbrev>
+++++
+
+experimental::[]
+
+The `random_sampler` aggregation is a single bucket aggregation that randomly
+includes documents in the aggregated results. Sampling provides significant
+speed improvement at the cost of accuracy.
+
+The sampling is accomplished by providing a random subset of the entire set of
+documents in a shard. If a filter query is provided in the search request, that
+filter is applied over the sampled subset. Consequently, if a filter is
+restrictive, very few documents might match; therefore, the statistics might not
+be as accurate.
+
+NOTE: This aggregation is not to be confused with the
+<<search-aggregations-bucket-sampler-aggregation,sampler aggregation>>. The
+sampler aggregation is not over all documents; rather, it samples the first `n`
+documents matched by the query.
+
+[source,console]
+----
+GET kibana_sample_data_ecommerce/_search?size=0&track_total_hits=false
+{
+  "aggregations": {
+    "sampling": {
+      "random_sampler": {
+        "probability": 0.1
+      },
+      "aggs": {
+        "price_percentiles": {
+          "percentiles": {
+            "field": "taxful_total_price"
+          }
+        }
+      }
+    }
+  }
+}
+----
+// TEST[setup:kibana_sample_data_ecommerce]
+
+[[random-sampler-top-level-params]]
+==== Top-level parameters for random_sampler
+
+`probability`::
+(Required, float) The probability that a document will be included in the
+aggregated data. Must be greater than 0, less than `0.5`, or exactly `1`. The
+lower the probability, the fewer documents are matched.
+
+`seed`::
+(Optional, integer) The seed to generate the random sampling of documents. When
+a seed is provided, the random subset of documents is the same between calls.
+
+[[random-sampler-inner-workings]]
+==== How does the sampling work?
+
+The aggregation is a random sample of all the documents in the index. In other
+words, the sampling is over the background set of documents. If a query is
+provided, a document is returned if it is matched by the query and if the
+document is in the random sampling. The sampling is not done over the matched
+documents.
+
+Consider the set of documents `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`. Your query matches `[1, 3, 5]`
+and the randomly sampled set is `[2, 4, 5]`. In this case, the document returned
+would be `[5]`.
+
+This type of sampling provides almost linear improvement in query latency in relation to the amount
+by which sampling reduces the document set size:
+
+image::images/aggregations/random-sampler-agg-graph.png[Graph of the median speedup by sampling factor,align="center"]
+
+This graph is typical of the speed up for the majority of aggregations for a test data set of 63 million documents. The exact constants will depend on the data set size and the number of shards, but the form of the relationship between speed up and probability holds widely. For certain aggregations, the speed up may not
+be as dramatic. These aggregations have some constant overhead unrelated to the number of documents seen. Even for
+those aggregations, the speed improvements can be significant.
+
+The sample set is generated by skipping documents using a geometric distribution
+(`(1-p)^(k-1)*p`) with success probability being the provided `probability` (`p` in the distribution equation).
+The values returned from the distribution indicate how many documents to skip in
+the background. This is equivalent to selecting documents uniformly at random. It follows that the expected number of failures before a success is
+`(1-p)/p`. For example, with the `"probability": 0.01`, the expected number of failures (or
+average number of documents skipped) would be `99` with a variance of `9900`.
+Consequently, if you had only 80 documents in your index or matched by your
+filter, you would most likely receive no results.
+
+image::images/aggregations/relative-error-vs-doc-count.png[Graph of the relative error by sampling probability and doc count,align="center"]
+
+In the above image `p` is the probability provided to the aggregation, and `n` is the number of documents matched by whatever
+query is provided. You can see the impact of outliers on `sum` and `mean`, but when many documents are still matched at
+higher sampling rates, the relative error is still low.
+
+NOTE: This represents the result of aggregations against a typical positively skewed APM data set which also has outliers in the upper tail. The linear dependence of the relative error on the sample size is found to hold widely, but the slope depends on the variation in the quantity being aggregated. As such, the variance in your own data may
+      cause relative error rates to increase or decrease at a different rate.

While working on this proposal, I found it's fragile. We need to carefully set and unset the point-in-time when updating the indices. Below is one of our usages that can be an issue. If we don't unset the `point-in-time` before retrieving `indices()` then we can add extra index filters to the search request although the actual indices can be empty.

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/273eeddc14601988ad0a70f0b199d163c6e09f1d/x-pack/plugin/eql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/eql/execution/search/PITAwareQueryClient.java#L105-L110

> Though I'd rather add the new base method to ActionRequestinstead of TransportAction because calling ActionRequest#validate() and ActionRequest#prepare() in sequence seems to be more fluent to me (it would be nice to make ActionRequest#prepare idempotent).

Now I think we should go with Yang's proposal.

> While working on this proposal, I found it's fragile. We need to carefully set and unset the point-in-time when updating the indices.

IIUC, the issue is that changing `point-in-time` for a `SearchRequest` also leads to change of the output from `SearchRequest.indices()`. This interaction could be unexpected and depending on the order of calls, the resulted `indices` can be different. If you want to use the `indices` subsequently in other places, it might not do what you meant to do.

If we could prevent setting `pointInTimeBuilder` when the `SearchRequest` has non-empty `indices`, would that help? In theory, it makes sense to prevent it from happening since we are already preventing it at the REST (API) layer. That said, I am aware it might be technically challenging since `SearchSourceBuider` does _not_ know about `SearchRequest`?

Nhat and I have discussed this and I was hoping that we could find a simpler, less intrusive solution for this problem. Given that the transport client is no longer around, we should not design our system for direct access to the transport layer, hence I would opt for adapting the search request setup on the client side to set the indices in addition to the point in time.
We decided not to proceed with this change, closing.
